title: Trias - Indie Deckbuilder - Is this the right way to communicate AI use?
author: AndreaNedra
selftext:
Hello! My name is Andrea and I'm one of the two developers behind the game.  
  
I'm here to ask for feedback on my communication as an indie game artist using AI to develop a game on [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4639070/Trias/).  
I've also included a timelapse showing the entire workflow.

I don't have strong illustration skills, so I find AI generated art extremely useful as a starting point, then I refine, edit and correct the sloppiness of the image generation.  
Without AI or a significant art budget, this game would be nearly impossible for us to create, due to the nature of the game, where card art reflects equipped items and its heavy reliance on a large number of card illustrations.

Just to have some number: Right now, we have 33 cards. With 5 weapon variations per card, that becomes 165 unique illustrations (33 × 5). At a conservative estimate of 4 hours per illustration, that's 660 hours of work. At a modest freelance rate of $30/hour, the total cost would be around $19,800 (660 × $30). We simply don't have that kind of budget.

I understand why many gamers are frustrated when large companies use AI simply to cut costs, often at the expense of quality and the overall player experience.

That's why I wanted to be as transparent as possible on our Steam page, explaining both why and how we use AI. My hope is that, by providing context and being open about our workflow, people can better understand the reasoning behind our use of generative AI.

Also since there's very little, almost no marketing budget and the wishlist growth is slow, is it worth the risk for a game like this to attract more attention, knowing that it might lose around 50% of its potential audience because of the AI usage?  
  
Are there any other studies on the impact of nuance of AI games?  
  
If you also have a game that uses AI, I'd be curious to hear about your experience communicating that to players and how it has impacted your game on Steam.

I'm looking forward to hearing your thoughts on it, thanks!

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
That's fine, but you came to an AI sub and wrote a whole post about how you're using AI in the production process, with an emphasis specifically on how to *show* those Anti-AI people that you're not making "slop" while discussing disclosure.

Why your wishlist growth is so slow is a totally separate discussion that has nothing to do with your AI dev pipeline, meanwhile everything you wrote in the OP is exclusively targeting appeasing those Anti-AI people under the assumption that they are why your wishlist uptick is not where you want it.  Like you specifically asked if your project is even worth continuing if "50%" of your potential audience is going to refuse to play it unless they're appeased.

Your wishlist growth is bad for two reasons:

1) You're an unknown studio making *yet another roguelike deckbuilder* when literally every indie and their mother is making a roguelike deckbuilder trying to chase the Slay The Spire money fountain.  That market space is completely and totally saturated and so far you're not bringing anything new or interesting to the table.  You've got about 15 seconds to capture someone's attention and zero marketing budget, opening with "ROGUELIKE DECKBUILDER" as your opening sales pitch, and the focus on AI is not winning anyone's attention.

2) You're saying that you're not looking to start the AI argument, but... literally **every word of your steam description above the fold** is explicitly starting that argument.  You spend your entire Recent Events highlight, two full paragraphs, and a massive embedded art banner straight up justifying your AI use before you even say a *single word* about your game.  The only people not immediately clicking past that are the Anti-AI zealots who are now looking to pick a fight with you, and those people also aren't gonna buy your game.  
  
If you want more wishlists, cut \*all\* the AI argument crap from your Steam page.  Stop talking about it, stop making it a big thing.  Put your disclosure in the disclosure section and move on. Focus on the *game*, not appeasing the AI haters.

replies.author: AndreaNedra
replies.body:
I get your point and thank you so much for your comment. When I started showing the game the first thing I wanted to do was distance myself as much as possible from those who try to hide their use of AI, so I built my communication around transparency.

Maybe it comes across as a little provocative toward the anti AI crowd, but my real goal is to show an ethical, middle ground approach using AI as a tool. I want to start a conversation about what I believe is a responsible way to use it, as a way to fill a skill gap and as a new pipeline that can make indie game development more affordable.

In your opinion, how could I improve the trailer?

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
>Maybe it comes across as a little provocative toward the anti AI crowd, but my real goal is to show an ethical, middle ground approach using AI as a tool. I want to start a conversation about what I believe is a responsible way to use it, as a way to fill a skill gap and as a new pipeline that can make indie game development more affordable.

Your steam page, and your trailer simply aren't the place to do that.  Your steam page and your trailer serve one purpose - to make a sales pitch for your game in a sea of hundreds of thousands of other games.  Debate on ethics of AI is an important topic, but that's the wrong audience.

How I would improve the trailer:  

* Cut the "Roguelike deckbuilder" splash text, those kinds of SEO terms belong in the tags and the product text on the steam page, not in the trailer.
* Show some of the actual roguelike deckbuilding aspects, right now it's just 30 seconds of someone playing a card game the viewer doesn't know anything about.  Even your second trailer only shows about 3 seconds of the "roguelike" gameplay as if its an afterthought.  And there's no "deckbuilding" anywhere to be found. Watching someone play a card game simply *isn't visually interesting*.  A big part of Slay The Spire's success is that the card play is actually extremely minimized in the design - you're watching visuals play out across most of the screen, the cards themselves are simply a stylization on selecting your actions each round.  Here's the one of the trailers for Roguebook, notice how little of it is focused on reading and playing cards, despite that being the crux of the whole game: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EaF6hb-m5Js](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EaF6hb-m5Js)
* The part where you equip a sword onto the card and show how the card itself changes?  That's a great hook, keep that.  You want more moments like that where you show instead of telling.  It also emphasizes how your game is *different* from others in the genre which is critical.
* There's english grammar and syntax errors in your trailer, fix them ASAP.  Remember you've got 15-30 seconds to hook someone on your game, and nothing turns people off faster than catching those errors when the gameplay is like 90% reading text. It makes it look like it lacks polish.

replies.author: AndreaNedra
replies.body: Thank you so much for your feedback, I will try to make a different trailer, also the game has more mechanics that are still in developing and some part are need more polish and visual feedback, so maybe is better to have first a more complete game in order to make a really good trailer, but we wanted to have a steam page as soon as possible so we can start collecting wishlist.

replies.author: MineDesperate8982
replies.body:
You're wasting time. This dude acts exactly how he claims the anti-ai people are acting.

For me, and a lot of other people, from what I've seen, it's not about the game using AI as a tool in its development.

It's about making AI slop and bragging about it.

There's a difference between AI slop products and products that use AI in development.

Did you just prompt some shit and told your LLM of choice "make me a game like x" without any actual effort being put in testing it, refining it, building on top of if and making it your own? That's AI slop.

And to add further insult to injury, a lot of them price it like a "normal" developed game, where the effort put in to it is astronomically smaller.

And, while I'm not really active in this sub, a lot of what people are doing here is just slop.

What's the difference between AI slop and slop made by some game studios? Only one, the game studio employs multiple people and contributes to the general economy. Otherwise, it's just slop with extra steps.

And this is where the whole issue with AI gen content came from - massive corporations laying off tens of thousands of people to replace them with AI, then create absolute slop products.

No sane person will have an issue with a small/single developer using AI to create their product. Sure, there are schizos, but schizos are in every possible walk of life.

You cannot afford to pay an artist or devs or whatever? That's fine. Do what you gotta do get your vision out. But at some point, I would recommend at least trying to understand what you're doing and why you're doing that, especially on the dev side.

You don't have to know game development, but at least try, in time, to learn how to understand what the code does. Imagine you're a product manager for said game studio. You don't don't have to know game dev, as a product manager, but it makes it easier to find solutions for issues, understand issues and come up with better workflows and such if you at least understand, broadly, what the code is doing - it will help you a lot.

You are the DJ Khaled of your project - the better you understand what you need and where you need it, the better the end-product is.

  
I've whishlisted the game not because I'm interested in this types of games, I'm not, but just to encourage you - I see you're putting in work and are actually interested in making a good product and I can appreciate that.

And also just to spite this dude, as a generally anti-AI games person.

How much are you thinking of pricing it?

\----

As a side note, about the whishlisting, where did you get that 50% figure from? Because I think you are facing other issues, more prevalent than the openness of AI usage (which is not a bad thing - people appreciate you being open, especially when you deliver a good product):

\- You don't have anything else in your library;

\- You are an unknown game studio;

\- You are already facing a pretty niche genre;

It's already pretty hard to "get going" as a game creator, no matter if you use AI or not or you are transparent about it or not. Starting off as a game creator with a card trading game is going to be even harder.

I think getting a demo out on steam for people to actually play test might be a good starting point.

Even better, get an alpha/beta out and make a discord channel for people to actually interact with you and report bugs or feedback.

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
There's two separate issues here:

1) Yes, 80-90% of what people are making with AI \*is trash\*.  No argument there, people are shoveling slop faster than they ever have before AI.  That margin was trash before too, now there's just more people enabled to make it.  Generally speaking you're right, most people who "want to make a video game" have no talent for design or technical knowledge to build quality games, same as it ever was.  

2) However, the anti-AI crusaders have nothing to do with that group.  \*Those\* are the people being discussed, the ones who sit on reddit all day wanking themselves off like they're some sort of freedom fighters for spending 8 hours a day finding any and every post and comment about AI to start frothing at the mouth fights over.  These people \*also\* make up 80-90% of all *discourse* about AI on the internet.

Sometimes the two intersect, but when they don't it still rings true.  That second group is who OP is targeting with their video, and that second group could be (and *has been, repeatedly)* handed the Illustrator files definitively proving something is not made with any amount of generative AI technology and they'll immediately throw it in the garbage so they can yell "SLOP, SLOP, SLOP" and wave their pitchforks even higher.  The analogy of the Salem Witch Trials is invoked so frequently with these people because of how apt it is, they're putting people through a constant gauntlet of unwinnable purity tests to justify their own preconceived biases.

comments.author: AngelOfLastResort
comments.body:
Like another poster said, your slow wishlist growth has nothing to do with your usage of AI. You need to work on your marketing skills - your trailer lacks oomph and your text is all about AI. You need to convince people to part with their hard earned cash. I get that you want to be honest, and there is space for that, but the identity of your game can't be "made with AI but not slop". That's not an identity. That's not something you can market or sell. People won't give you money for that.

Also, look I'm not the target market for your game. I played Slay the Spire a bit, like did a few runs, nothing major. But Slay the Spire is not just cards. Cards are how the player makes decisions - the game backgrounds shows you the consequences of your decisions through animation. Your game background is... a table. That's it. A table.

Like I said, I'm not your target audience, but I think you have some work to do, and stop blaming anti AI bias for your slow wishlist growth. Take a real long hard look at what you've got.
